report:
The evidence does **not** clearly support a "yes" answer. While some smaller studies suggest benefit, the most authoritative and largest studies find little to no effect.

**Evidence against efficacy (stronger):**

- The **Cochrane systematic review** (2022, updated from 2013) pooled data from four trials totaling 1,543 participants and concluded that "there was no evidence that Ginkgo biloba is effective for tinnitus when this is the primary complaint." Pooled data showed ginkgo "may have little to no effect" on tinnitus severity compared to placebo, with very uncertain evidence. ([Cochrane](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003852_ginkgo-biloba-tinnitus); [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36383762/))

- The **largest trial to date** (1,121 participants, double-blind, placebo-controlled, published in BMJ) found that ginkgo extract LI 1370 "had no greater therapeutic effect than placebo in treating tinnitus." ([PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC26593/))

**Evidence suggesting possible benefit (weaker):**

- A **systematic review** of randomized, placebo-controlled trials found evidence of efficacy specifically for the standardized extract EGb 761® in three trials, though it noted results vary across studies and extracts. ([PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3157487/))

- A recent **open-label (uncontrolled) study** of 170 patients reported improvements with EGb 761® over 24 weeks, but lacked a placebo group, limiting conclusions. ([MDPI](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/15/1/87))

**Bottom line:** The highest-quality evidence — the Cochrane review and the largest RCT — does not support ginkgo extract as an effective treatment for tinnitus. Some smaller, often lower-quality studies with the specific EGb 761® extract suggest possible benefit, but the overall balance of evidence leans toward little to no effect. Your assumption of "yes" is not well supported by the best available evidence.
